title: I Built 3 SaaS Companies in a Row to Prove It's Not Luck…
normalization: Concatenate utf8 segments per caption event; retain event start and duration; whitespace trim only.

segments.text: I've bootstrapped three SaaS companies
from zero to millions of dollars in
revenue. My first startup was Robly,
which took 17 months and 25 people to
scale to seven figures, and I eventually
sold it for 10 million. My second was
GetEmails, which took only 27 weeks and
six [music] people to hit a million, and
now it's sitting at 21 million ARR as
retention.com. My third, RBDDB, took
just 16 weeks and five people, and now
it's at 8 million ARR and still growing.
Every single time it was twice as fast
with half the resources. A lot of people
look at a track record like that and
say, "Well, he just got lucky three
times." I want to make this video to
prove that it's not luck, it's a skill.
And in the next few minutes, I'm going
to break down exactly what I did
differently each time so you can start
applying the same thing to whatever
you're building right now. My first
venture was Robly, and I never built a
product before starting it. Going from
idea to getting our first paying
customer took two and a half years.
Robly was an email marketing platform.
Think about Mailchimp or Constant
Contact. We were competing in that space
with a $35 a month product. The entire
business is sales-led. I was writing the
sales scripts myself. I was managing the
sales people. At one point, I had 38
people showing up in my apartment every
day, smiling and dialing. Not only was
it a grind, it was a really slow, brutal
grind. Now, our growth strategy was
actually pretty clever for the time.
Before data enrichment tools or AI, we
scraped the internet for Constant
Contact signup forms. If a company had
one of those forms on their website, we
knew that they were a potential
customer. We enriched that list with
phone numbers and called them with a
better offer, 50% more opens at half the
price. That was the entire pitch. And
this worked until it didn't. We hit 3
million ARR and completely stalled out.
Mailchimp had a free product and a
better product, and we just couldn't
compete. We ended up selling the company
to a PE firm in 2020 for $10 million.
But while I was trying to figure out how
to grow Robly, we found something
interesting. We came across a technology
that could resolve anonymous website
visitors into deliverable email
addresses. My original plan was to use
it as a feature inside of Robly to help
customers grow their list, but that plan
changed very quickly. The second venture
was GetEmails, which is now called
retention.com. So, when we launched the
website visitor identity feature inside
of Robly, something unexpected happened.
The user experience was horrible. People
had to manually download a file and
upload it into Klaviyo themselves.
Despite that, they were giving us a 10
on our net promoter scores. When someone
tolerates a painful process and still
says your product is awesome, that's a
signal you can't ignore. That's when I
had the epiphany. This shouldn't be a
feature inside of an email newsletter
app. It needed to be its own standalone
product, connected to everything, and
usable with any email platform. That
became GetEmails, which is now called
retention.com. This time around, the
numbers look very different. It took us
27 weeks to hit a million ARR from
November 19 to April 2020, and we only
had six people. The growth engine was
Facebook ads driving 15-minute demos.
Someone on our team ran thousands of
demos. These ads were unlike anything
else running in the space at the time.
Instagram stories and Snapchat were
blowing up, and people were walking
around making these short, funny videos
with props and different backgrounds. I
thought, "What if I did that, but
instead it was an ad for my company? 1
minute, one new one every week,
answering a sales question." But it was
me and my wife with props and different
backgrounds every time. My philosophy
was, "If people start expecting your ad,
you've won the game." And that's exactly
what happened. Those ads worked for
about 6 months before they stopped
scaling. We'd run the ads, bringing a
bunch of tiny customers, and then one
big spender would come in and spend
$5,000 for 1 month. That one customer
would pay back all the ad spend. That
model ran for 6 months, and by then we
had enough momentum to keep going by
relying on other channels. We eventually
got retention.com to 13 million ARR with
six people, mostly cold email and word
of mouth after the ads stopped. Now, the
company's at 21 million ARR. The third
company's RBDDB. While trying to grow
retention.com in the Shopify space, I
started posting on LinkedIn. The goal
was to reach Shopify store owners, but
my content kept going viral with B2B
SaaS founders instead. I noticed that
nobody was offering person-level website
visitor identity for B2B companies. I
had two things colliding at the same
time. A large, engaged B2B audience
built completely organically on
LinkedIn, and number two was a gap in
the market for a product I already knew
how to build and was selling to the
Shopify space. That became RBDDB. I came
up with the idea in the fall of 2022,
built it in the winter of 2023, and then
launched on March 12th, 2023. 16 weeks
later, we hit 1 million ARR. It was only
five people on the team, and the entire
growth strategy was founder-led content
on LinkedIn and nothing else. No paid
ads, no sales team, just content. This
felt completely different than Robly.
Robly was a grind. It was me running a
sales team. It was 38 people smiling and
dialing, whereas RBDDB was this massive
thought leadership funnel that flowed
into this freemium PLG that didn't
involve sales at all. The business today
runs on three people and AI. AI handles
all of the customer support, pre-signup
and post-signup. A human looks at maybe
one out of every 50 tickets, and when
they do, their entire job is to
eliminate that category of ticket so AI
doesn't have to answer it again. What
used to take 38 people in my apartment
now takes three. And by the way, if you
want to see exactly how RBDDB changes
things completely for B2B signups, you
can sign up for free at the first link
in the description. We push the LinkedIn
profiles of your anonymous website
visitors directly into Slack so you can
reach out to them while they're still
hot. Now, let me share with you my
biggest takeaway. The takeaway is
startups are hard. I'm not going to
sugarcoat that. Robly was years of cold
calls, a product that stalled, and a
sale that was fine, but not what I had
originally imagined. But that difficulty
was the education that I needed. The
longer you do this, the more skilled you
become at the craft. You get better at
finding your leverage and just pressing
on it. You get more efficient with
people, money, and time, and that
definitely isn't luck. The numbers show
exactly what compounding looks like. The
first time, it took me 17 months and 25
people to hit 1 million ARR. The second
time, it was 27 weeks and six people.
And the third time, it was just 16 weeks
and five people. Each swing you take,
you get closer to it. So, if you're in
the middle of something right now, and
it feels impossibly hard, keep going and
keep building. And if you want to make
scaling a little easier, that's exactly
what RBDDB is built for. It shows you
who's already visiting your website and
showing interest in your product, and
it's completely free. That's the kind of
leverage I wish I had when I started.
So, if you want to try it out for free,
click the first link in the description.
And if you want to see the exact AI
funnel that helped me scale to 8 million
ARR, then watch this video next.
